newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewsish settlers despair of Netanyahu as champion.
newsitem.headline: Jewsish settlers despair of Netanyahu as champion.

text.p: Jewish settlers who campaigned hard last year for Benjamin Netanyahu's election as Israel's prime minister on Tuesday called for the government to quit.
Settlers were outraged when Netanyahu's government, which took office in June, handed 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule on January 17.

"I just think that (regarding) the current government, we made a mistake when we called for supporting it and it needs to end its term as soon as possible," Pinchas Wallerstein, chairman of the umbrella council of Jewish settlers, told Israel Radio.
The Hebron handover was an ideological U-turn for Netanyahu who had always opposed the land-for-peace formula with the Palestine Liberation Organisation, a group he branded terrorist.
Wallerstein could barely control his rage at Netanyahu's resumption of the peace process along lines laid down by the centre-left government which the Likud party leader ousted.
"This government has misled the people," he said.
Settlers believe what they call the Greater Land of Israel, including the Gaza Strip and West Bank occupied by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war, is the Jewish people's by biblical right.
Palestinians want some day to establish a state in the areas where 130,000 settlers live amidst two million Palestinians.
Jewish settlers now feel their dream is under threat. Netanyahu has not approved any new settlements, pledging only to expand existing ones.

Addenda to the Hebron deal set out a timetable for further withdrawals from rural areas of the West Bank. Israel's previous government handed seven West Bank towns and some 400 villages to Palestinian rule.
Calling for the government's fall appeared to be an act of desperation by the settlers.

Only two parties have ever headed a government in Israel -- Netanyahu's Likud or the dovish Labour. Thus the alternative to a Likud-led coalition could be Labour -- or Netanyahu might solve a coalition crisis by entering a national unity government with Labour. Both options would work against the settlers.
But settlers hope a new standard-bearer would emerge within the Likud if Netanyahu is ousted.

Benny Begin, son of the late Likud founder and former prime minister Menachem Begin, resigned his post as science minister over the Hebron deal last month. But Wallerstein said it was too early to say if Begin would consent to be the man of the hour.
Bringing down the government is a long shot in any event.

The National Religious Party (NRP), the staunchest champion of settlement of occupied Arab lands in Netanyahu's coalition, on Tuesday denied media reports it had abandoned the "Greater Land of Israel" ideal.

Party spokesman Yehoshua Mor-Yosef said the nine NRP members of parliament, many of whom are settlers, would from Wednesday no longer participate in parliament votes until Netanyahu approved building more homes for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem.
He said nothing of leaving the coalition over East Jerusalem, much less over areas in the rest of the West Bank. Netanyahu with NRP commands 66 seats in the 120-seat parliament.
Mor-Yosef denied a report in Israel's Maariv daily that the NRP had abandoned fighting for the entire "Land of Israel".

But he admitted NRP members had to work with the present reality in the West Bank. He said they had met to discuss strategy on the basis of the current map of the West Bank in which parts of the land are ruled by the PLO.
